title: What this recorded session shows
narration: This is a longer walk through of the actual Survive Drive interface. You will see the controls respond, the candidate cards rerank, and the map and lookup count change as we work. One disclosure before we begin: this Los Angeles training file contains invented route lines, travel times, and property values. It is not a live California Valhalla search. The local routing graph does not yet cover California, and no paid property lookup will run during this recording. The point is to learn the sequence and the decisions you control. Notice the training banner at the top throughout this recording. I am working through the same panels a driver would use, but the example route evidence is deliberately fenced off from live services. When we reach a control that would request paid information, I will stop at its preview. That distinction matters because the app's estimates are useful only when you can tell what is saved, what is unknown, and what a new call would add.

title: Set both ends of the trip
narration: I start in Set the trip. For this exercise, I name the start Santa Clarita and the destination Long Beach, then enter their area coordinates. These points are for training, not exact door to door addresses. You can also place the S and D pins on the map. Watch how the map responds as the second point arrives. No routing or property service is called by typing these settings. A real trip deserves precise points, because even a short move can change which roads are available and which cells a route crosses. The two names are labels that help me recognize the trip later; the coordinates are what place the endpoints. I pause on this screen because the rest of the workflow inherits these choices. If either endpoint is wrong, it is better to correct it before generating gates or routes than to reason carefully about the wrong journey. The buttons in the left rail make the sequence visible, so I can move back before committing to a search.

title: Choose road preferences
narration: Next I review what Valhalla should favor. The route preference can emphasize faster travel or a balance of time and distance. The baseline limit allows up to four alternatives when no Escape Gates are used. Further down are highway and toll road preferences, ferry choices, unpaved roads, cash only tolls, and H O V eligibility. These are instructions to the route engine, not a promise that every unwanted road can be avoided. Only select an H O V occupancy you actually meet. This version does not use live traffic, so treat the time estimates as planning estimates. Watch the settings themselves, rather than assuming a single avoid switch guarantees a particular road. Avoidance is usually a preference in a constrained road network. A bridge, turn restriction, or disconnected local street can force a compromise. The app exposes these parameters so you can make that tradeoff before requesting a potentially large cross product of route candidates. If you alter them after a search, you should expect to generate a new candidate batch and revisit the cost forecast for evidence.

title: Understand Escape Gates
narration: Escape Gates suggest different ways to leave the starting area and approach the destination. Here are the inner and outer radii, maximum suggestions, and separation controls. In a live California search, G O would ask for road suggestions near both ends, using saved Census road circles when available. We do not press G O in this training recording: the next step loads an illustrative candidate file, and I will not imply invented gates came back from Census. The full route batch includes every selected start and destination combination, plus each no gate choice. Four selected gates at each end would mean five times five, or twenty five pairings. The inner and outer distances define the annulus where suggestions are considered, and the separation control keeps nearby suggestions from piling onto effectively the same road. More gates increase exploration, but their start and destination counts multiply. This is why I check the batch before starting. A moderate choice at each end can still become many route requests. In this tutorial the gate screen is a real app screen; only the later imported candidate file is illustrative.

title: Load the clearly labeled training file
narration: Now I use Load saved routes to bring the exercise into the real app. The banner stays on screen so you can tell this is illustrative data. The browser reads the file locally. It makes no Valhalla or RentCast call. You can see four candidate cards and the route map appear. Their lines are schematic, not road matched; the displayed times and property values were invented for teaching. The generic imported route label is not evidence that HERE or Valhalla returned them. In your own trip, this is where real Valhalla results would replace the training file. The import is useful for reviewing a previous session, too. Here I use that mechanism to teach the controls without invoking a service. A saved file is evidence of what was in that file, not proof that a provider just answered. Read the training label before interpreting any map line. The route map is a visual aid for comparing four options, while the cards show the separate evidence fields that will drive ranking and selection.

title: Run the free Round 0 screen
narration: I open Evaluate and apply a Red Cell threshold of two hundred dollars per square foot. Red means a known cell falls below that threshold. The app then checks its mapped cells and available values, and completes Round zero without a new paid property lookup. This exercise uses an isolated training cache, so the values on screen are still examples. Round zero ranks all four candidates. With a thirty five percent cull setting, rounding leaves two nominal INCLUDED slots here. A candidate under twenty percent known coverage is protected from this first cull. Notice that an EXCLUDED route stays visible in the ranking. Unknown evidence is not a low property value. This is the economical starting point. The app first asks what can be inferred from information already in hand. It counts mapped eligible cells, looks up saved values, and ranks before proposing any new AVM call. The protection rule prevents a route with very little known coverage from being discarded merely because its few known cells look poor. Still, protection does not make that route good; it marks the evidence as thin enough to warrant caution. The first cull changes who is eligible for more sampling, and the ranking continues to show the complete field.

title: Read the ranking and compare routes
narration: Look across the four ranked cards before you commit to another round. Each shows travel distance and time, known coverage, unknown cells, known Red share, and weighted price per square foot. The route with the lowest known Red share ranks first. When Red shares tie, higher weighted price per square foot is the next sort key. I select another card and the map switches to that candidate, then return to the first. Coverage matters: a low Red percentage based on very little known distance is less informative than a similar result with broad coverage. Live Valhalla routes exclude highway runs and attached ramps from this property comparison. This schematic file does not prove highway classification. I read the status line and the evidence numbers together. A count of unknown cells tells me how much of the path still lacks property evidence. Known coverage tells me the fraction that is actually being compared. The weighted price is a summary of known mapped cells and should not be read as a quotation for any particular house. When I click a different candidate, the highlighted line and card change together. That is the point of this review: see whether the apparent leader remains attractive once its time, path, and uncertainty are considered.

title: Read and adjust the honeycomb
narration: The route and its colored honeycomb can now be inspected together. The red threshold stays at two hundred. I narrow the map's upper color bound from five hundred to four hundred fifty dollars per square foot, and the color contrast changes. That upper bound is a display control. It does not change the route ranking or make an A V M request. Gray cells are unknown, not safe or unsafe. These property estimates describe geographic value; they are not a safety rating for people, homes, or neighborhoods. In a real session, look for highway entry and exit cues and check what each colored cell actually covers. Color is easy to overread, so I treat the honeycomb as a prompt to inspect rather than a verdict. The lower threshold determines which known eligible cells count as Red for this run. The upper value stretches the display scale so a narrow local range is easier to see. I can change that display without consuming credits. I also leave unknown cells visible; hiding them would make a sparse route look more certain than it is. On a real road matched route, the highway exclusion keeps highway distance from diluting the local-road comparison.

title: Choose who receives more evidence
narration: Now I change the next evidence pool. I exclude the first candidate, then include the second one. Both remain visible in the ranking, and the forecast changes as the INCLUDED set changes. This is a substitution decision, not a permanent deletion of routes. The app can promote a previously EXCLUDED candidate after later evidence changes the full ranking. A protected low coverage route survived Round zero, but I can still adjust the next round deliberately. These buttons control which candidates may receive new property evidence; they do not select a driving route for me. Here the distinction between rank and inclusion matters. Rank is the current order across candidates. Inclusion says who receives the next sample, so I can move that sampling attention without erasing a candidate. The automatic cull uses a percentage of the current nominal pool after each round, and the top-ranked candidates refill the remaining slots. A previously excluded route can therefore return as the evidence changes. I make a manual substitution on screen and watch the projected lookup count update; the new cost calculation must follow the latest inclusion state.

title: Calculate the exact One Round count
narration: The per route count starts at five unknown cells. I briefly lower it to three, see the forecast shrink, and restore five. Then I select Calculate exact One Round lookups. The app checks this isolated training cache, chooses the exact cells, and removes duplicates shared by candidates. For this invented exercise, the prepared plan is nine new lookups, or nine credits at one cent each. That is not a price quote for a real Los Angeles trip. Calculating the count is separate from Run one Manual round. I do not press Run. Instead, I change the count again, which clears the prepared plan. No paid lookup has happened. This is the last free checkpoint before a paid round. The estimate beside the control responds immediately to the per-route count and the INCLUDED set, but the exact plan performs a cache check and deduplicates the chosen cells. I read both the count and the credits before deciding whether to spend them. One credit is one cent in the current display. A failed provider attempt may still count against the provider ceiling, so there is no automatic retry. The separate Run button is the commitment point. In this recording I deliberately stop before it and then edit the count, demonstrating that the old prepared plan is invalidated.

title: Look around before choosing
narration: With the cost plan cleared, I move to Look around. This panel lets you inspect mapped cells, record your own assessment, and choose an inspection point for Street View. I place a sample point and show the Street View control without opening a panorama in this recording. If you use it, check the image capture date; imagery can be old or missing. Record what you actually observe separately from the property value signal. For a real route, compare uncertainty and road conditions as well as time. A colored map alone is not enough to decide where you would drive. The inspection step is where I slow down and ask what the numerical screen did not tell me. A good looking price signal does not establish the condition of a road, and a map color cannot describe lighting, construction, or a difficult interchange. Street View can help orient a person, but the photographs are only snapshots of particular dates and viewpoints. I place an inspection marker so the app can retain that point. I would add notes only for observations I can actually support, especially if I intend to compare this route with another later.

title: Record and export a decision
narration: Finally I open Choose or adjust. I type a short reason and record a sample choice inside this local exercise. This is a saved comparison decision, not turn by turn navigation. You can export the session if you want to preserve the settings, candidate evidence, and notes. On a real trip I would first obtain genuine routes, consider where the evidence remains unknown, and decide whether another priced One Round is worthwhile. Survive Drive is meant to make those tradeoffs visible while you remain in control. That completes the screen recorded workflow. The saved reason is useful because after several rounds it is easy to forget why a route looked preferable. I can mention travel time, known coverage, unknown segments, and the places I inspected. The app preserves alternatives so the choice remains revisable if a new fact appears. It is also possible to stop without buying another round when the current evidence is enough for your purpose. In a real trip, I would review the route in a navigation tool and current road conditions before driving. This training recording ends with a recorded example choice and no charged lookup.
